Release: llm-gemini 0.37 Google launched Gemini 4 Hydrogen today - the lowest cost member of the Gemini 4 family.

It's actually not…
blogs.content:
Release: llm-gemini 0.37

 Google launched Gemini 4 Hydrogen today - the lowest cost member of the Gemini 4 family.

 It's actually not too far off the price of its much bigger siblings, Carbon and Argon. I'm finding Gemini 4's pricing really confusing. Here's the pricing scheme:

 Model
 Dates
 Input ($/M)
 Cached input
 Output

 Gemini 4 Carbon
 Through Nov 30, 2026
 $2.00
 $0.10

 From Dec 1, 2026

 $0.20

 Gemini 4 Argon
 Through Nov 30, 2026
 $2.00
 $0.10
 $10.00

 From Dec 1, 2026
 $4.00
 $0.20
 $20.00

 Gemini 4 Hydrogen
  
 $1.50
 $0.075
 $7.50

 Carbon and Argon are the same price , and both are scheduled to double in price on December 1st. If they're the same price, why have two different models? Google says that Argon "delivers Gemini 4 intelligence with faster responses and lower token spend per turn compared to Gemini 4 Carbon" - so it may be priced the same, but it will use less tokens per task.

 Hydrogen, supposedly the cheap model, is currently only a 25% discount on its more capable peers. The Hydrogen price will make more sense after December 1st, when it will represent a 75% discount. It's still considerably more expensive than Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6 Luna - they're both $0.10/$0.50, so Hydrogen is 15x that.

 I had Hydrogen generate some pelicans . Here's a full comparison grid showing the pelicans for all three members of the Gemini 4 family at their three supported effort levels:

 Considering how close they are in price, the difference in pelican quality for Hydrogen is quite stark.

 Here's how Google describe Hydrogen's intended position in their mix of models:

 In real-world software development, while teams rely on frontier models like Carbon and Argon for deep architectural judgment when designing systems or untangling subtle bugs, they still need a fast, disciplined execution model for writing code, running tests, and verifying changes. Hydrogen is built to stand on its own as a model for everyday work — or to pair with Carbon and Argon as the high-efficiency execution engine in multi-model workflows.

 Most notably, Hydrogen is the new free tier model, and is the model that will power AI features in Google Search.

blogs.content:
Release: llm 0.37.2

 Fixes a security issue reported by Daniel de Araujo in GHSA-v9h7-jj4g-f862 and GHSA-r639-rr7r-x72w .

 LLM has a mechanism called extra-openai-models.yaml - now managed by the new-in-0.37 llm openai endpoint add command - for using LLM with OpenAI-compatible API endpoints from other providers.

 Daniel reported two ways this could accidentally send your configured OpenAI API key to one of those providers: if the key named by api_key_name had never been stored, or if a responses: true model was run with -o chat_completions 1 .

blogs.description: Anthropic's IPO roadshow video Anthropic kicked off their IPO roadshow yesterday, and their roadshow video has some previously unreleased…
blogs.content:
Anthropic's IPO roadshow video

Anthropic kicked off their IPO roadshow yesterday, and their roadshow video has some previously unreleased information about how their business works.

 The section on "Approach to compute" with co-founder Tom Brown is particularly interesting, describing how Anthropic train and serve Claude across AWS Trainium, Google TPUs, NVIDIA GPUs, and AMD GPUs.

 I'm not sure why there's no official video transcript, but here's one that I extracted using MacWhisper. Highlights below:

 We train and serve Claude now across all four major chip families. That's only possible because early on we made an unconventional bet on a multi-chip strategy. At the time, many people thought that running AI models on different chips wasn't worth the effort. Each chip needs its own tailored software stack and inference stack, which is expensive and difficult to build. We've now been doing it for years, and we've gotten incredibly good at it. [...]

 As an example, this year, we started working with AMD GPUs for the first time. In the past, bringing on a new chip platform took dozens of engineers months of work This time, we had Mythos try it out. It got Claude running on AMD in just three days, with basically no human intervention . Claude ported or wrote almost 100% of the kernels. [...]

 The second driver of our compute advantage is our rate of discovery of compute multipliers. We focus on total effective compute, which is the multiplicative product of physical capacity times the compute multipliers that we discover. Each one we discover makes our pool of total effective compute bigger. For example, say you need 100 units of compute to train a model of a certain intelligence. A 4x compute multiplier means you can use 25 units of compute to train the exact same model. Or you can use those hundred physical units to train an even more intelligent model that would have previously required 400 units.

 Compute multipliers create a competitive advantage for us that's hard to replicate. They build on each other. Each new multiplier we discover has a positive effect on the multipliers before it. They stack. We believe that this can accelerate even further as we approach recursive self-improvement. Claude will be able to discover compute multipliers entirely by itself , allowing the number of compute multipliers to grow faster and faster.

 We got a hint at Anthropic's multi-chip strategy last September in their postmortem of three recent issues , where they described bugs that affected just their TPU deployments.

 Tags: ai , generative-ai , llms , anthropic , gpus , claude-mythos-fable , recursive-self-improvement

blogs.name: Stratechery by Ben Thompson
blogs.title: An Interview With Roblox CEO David Baszucki About Aggregating Play
blogs.author: Ben Thompson
blogs.description:
Listen to this post: Good morning,

This week’s Stratechery Interview is with Roblox CEO David Baszucki. I’ve interviewed…
blogs.content:
Listen to this post:

 Good morning,

 This week’s Stratechery Interview is with Roblox CEO David Baszucki . I’ve interviewed Baszucki twice, in February 2022 , and November 2023 .

 What struck me about this interview is just how much AI has changed the landscape for Roblox. This was a company predicated on the concept that anyone can make a game, but now, for the first time, literally anyone can make a game. That means a world of abundance, and in that world, there is an opportunity to be an Aggregator, and Roblox is aggressively pursuing that opportunity.

 To that end, we discuss how AI has changed Baszucki’s view of what is possible, what goes into a game creation harness, making games on your phone, and the power of recommendation. Then we talk about Roblox’s vision of a universal player, where a Roblox game works everywhere, and Roblox Everywhere, where Roblox developers can use the platform beyond the Roblox app. We also touch on advertising — the natural Aggregator business model — and whether Baszucki still thinks he is building the metaverse.

 As a reminder, all Stratechery content, including interviews, is available as a podcast; click the link at the top of this email to add Stratechery to your podcast player.

 On to the Interview:

 An Interview With Roblox CEO David Baszucki About Aggregating Play

 This interview is lightly edited for clarity.

 Topics: The AI Impact | A Game Creation Harness | Roblox Build | Roblox Discovery | Universal Player | Roblox Everywhere | Advertising | Metaverses

 The AI Impact

 David Baszucki, welcome back to Stratechery.

 DB: Thank you, Ben, for having me back. It’s great to be here.

 So this is the third time I’ve interviewed you, and I want to sort of put that in an interesting context. First, you started Roblox in 2004, you went public in 2021, you first talked to me in 2022 and again in 2023 , that’s like a nearly 20-year stretch. Now it’s 2026, and here’s my question: Is the world more different for you now, compared to three years before, than it was for the entire first two decades from starting the company to the last time we talked?

 DB: The changes in the world we all feel are sure happening a lot more rapidly. When we first published Roblox — I don’t know if people on this podcast remember — software used to be distributed on floppy disks and CDs.

 You know, the funny thing is, you’re the second person I’ve interviewed in the last two or three weeks where we’ve referenced back to fact that the reason we say packaged software is it used to actually be packaged!

 DB: It’s been crazy, we had the Internet, when we started the company, we had the vision of a category called immersive co-experience, sci-fi writers have been writing about the holodeck forever, and we went along our way.

 I’m still pro-metaverse, we can use the word metaverse, it’s okay.

 DB: Okay, good, we use them all. It’s Snow Crash — metaverse, holodeck, they’re all good. We started on this vision of building human co-experience, we saw the mobile age come across us, we saw the crypto age. The AI acceleration wave we’re in is faster and bigger and crazier than anything I’ve ever seen, it’s changing how we think about the product, it’s changing how people are going to create games. What’s really exciting is, when we started the company, we had this slogan called “You Make the Game”.

 Yep.

 DB: We started with that slogan, we learned along the way that the ratio of people who might want to play games to make games has drifted — more people want to just play games than make games, because historically making games has been Roblox Studio and 3D editing and writing script.

 We could be approaching the time where “You Make the Game” really comes true, and where making a game is accessible to everyone. It’s really fun, I’ll tell you a bit about some of the experiments we’ve been having with Roblox Build . But we’re entering an era where making a game could be as big as playing a game.

 I’m right there with you. We’re obviously going to touch on all those points, I think it’s probably predictable what we want to talk about. But to go back to 2023, you called AI then, “a super paintbrush and a super 3D modeler, rather than a full replacement” — Is that still how you’re thinking about AI?

 DB: It’s what the data is proving out. We just had our earnings call a few weeks ago , we highlighted a lot of acceleration. One, there’s various ways humans can augment with AI on Roblox, they can use MCP , which is like plugging in a model, they can use the Roblox AI assistant to help build.

 And what do you mean with that MCP server? You mentioned you had 5x growth quarter-over-quarter. That’s where you’re actually using Claude Code or Codex or whatever to work with Roblox?

 DB: People are plugging in, we can see all of them — Claude Code, Codex, other models — all being plugged into Roblox Studio to help build things. We’ve seen two games hit the top 20 made by AI, we have other metrics like the number of assets.

 What do you mean by “made by AI”? Because you also said 80% of games in the top 100 have AI-contributed content.

 DB: Touched by AI, vibe-coded directly with AI, and we can see the count of assets accelerating.

 Got it.

 DB: It’s turned out to be, I believe, somewhat faithful to what I said. This is a human paintbrush accelerator, good ideas are still very important, novel types of gameplay are very important. But people are able to flex their creativity much more quickly. We have members of the Roblox board of directors carrying a mobile phone around, building games like 15 times a day. We have people who are not necessarily engineers or product managers now building within the company, so we’re really at the dawn of a new era.

 A Game Creation Harness

 You mentioned the super paintbrush, super 3D modeler, is there a super gameplay developer? Because there’s a large step between, “I have an idea for a game”, versus the actual mechanics of the game. How much can the AI do to help you as far as that goes?

 DB: You’re touching on the dream of what is a game creation harness versus a coding harness .

 Dive into it, this is super interesting. Lay out the difference and the way you’re thinking about that.

 DB: So everyone’s getting familiar with coding harnesses — Claude Code, Cursor, Replit, Lovable, Codex, you name it. A game is arguably much more complicated than code. As you mentioned, there’s art, there’s 3D objects, there’s scenes, there’s avatars, there can be gameplay code, there can be missions, and there can be code underneath it. So a harness that is being created to create games really has to run in multiple modalities, needs to listen to you, and if you said, “I would like a multiplayer tortoise-and-the-hare game that 100 people can play, and we’d like to do it on Venus, and I’d like it to run on all devices” — there’s a lot of different things that need to be generated there.

 The avatars, the assets, all of that, as well as the gameplay, which I think is a very human thing — your idea of what type of a game it is is actually very unique. So one of our board members is building a hybrid kind of Wordle-crossword game with his own vision of how this crossword game should work, and that’s very unique to him. I’m optimistic we’re still seeing that notion of a human coupled with an accelerating paintbrush in essentially a very complex harness for building games.

 There’s so many pieces you talked about. The asset creation piece, compared to 2023, much further along, arguably there. You could have even the video component, or the moving worlds, but then you almost have these different pieces. Do you have to build — is there going to be one harness, and one sort of — we’re going to get to your Build app in a little bit — that handles all of that? Or are you still thinking we need to do this piece-by-piece as the model gets good enough for, or we need different models maybe for the different parts of this?

 DB: I think just as we see with harnesses that are routing different models, even for coding now, a lot of companies have multiple models running side-by-side and their harness is optimizing. Our harness inside Build and inside Studio Build is running not just multiple models for certain things, but then there’s a second dimension of, “Are we building a scene?”, “Are we building a 3D object?”, “Are we building code?”, “Are we building an NPC?”.

 So yes, we are routing both by kind of specific asset that’s being created, as well as multiple models within each of those, and we’re combining some areas where we have incredible data on Roblox — for example, data that can be used to help create non-player characters, characters that act normally, side-by-side with you. But there’s also really good coding models out there, both open source and frontier, and so we see a harness being able to put all these things together.

 What’s the mix of those models? Say we have three categories — frontier, off-the-shelf open-source models, and models that you’ve trained specifically. And I guess even there there’s two categories, are you doing foundational models on your own, or just doing some post-training?

 DB: We literally have all three of those running in our Build harness. And we’re, in certain cases, optimizing the cost of frontier with the capabilities of open source. We have a Cube model — we’ve announced it — which is trained on 3D assets.

 Yeah, super interesting. Tell me about the Cube model.

 DB: The Cube model is our own 3D asset creation model trained on all of the 3D objects inside Roblox, where the developer has opted in to the training. It’s very fast, it’s very efficient, and it runs on our own hardware. When you go into Build or I go into Build and I say, “Hey, make that tortoise-and-a-hare game”, and if you describe that tortoise as somewhat unique and different, “I want the tortoise to look like this, and have a fur that looks like this, and maybe have this”, that Cube model will and may come into play and generate that tortoise for you.

 How does your cost structure work for this? Is it a usage thing from a developer perspective? You have the MCP server — that’s where they can bring their own, what’s the mix?

 DB: You sound like a product manager, because these are exactly the same discussions I had about an hour ago. The ultimate vision is something like Roblox Build is just like the creation of short-form video. Short-form video 10 years ago — all of a sudden we all figured out we can make video and edit it on our phones, amongst multiple products that was like a huge revelation.

 We are so on the same page, I have a whole section on short-form video later in the interview. That’s good foreshadowing.

 DB: Yeah. And so along comes short-form video, and we have phones, and all of a sudden we’re making and sharing video. Arguably games are a lot more complicated, they can be immersive 3D environments, multiple people can come there. They have, as I was saying, code and geometry and avatars, but that’s where Build is going — that same notion of, “I’m going to pull out my phone and create something”, some of those models are still expensive.

 But the dream is, we’re already testing — I think Canada went live today. We’re testing in, I think, Serbia and New Zealand, we want it available for everyone and so it creates a wonderful opportunity for us to be super efficient with our models while super powerful. It creates the opportunity for those users who want to just do hundreds of iterations to have them buy tokens as well, if they really want to dig into it, so we’re optimistic this will be free for everyone.

 Roblox Build

 You keep mentioning Build, I’m on your website , and this is how you describe Build: “Build is a new way to make your own Roblox game right from your phone. Just describe the game you want in your own words, and Build’s AI creates a playable game for you in real time. You don’t need any coding or...

blogs.content:
Read Online | Sign Up | Advertise

 Good morning, {{ first_name | AI enthusiasts }}, and welcome to our 5,952 new readers. Jensen Huang has been Nvidia’s center of gravity since 1993, long enough to turn it into the engine of the entire AI boom. That run may suddenly be down to its final days.
 A new report says directors are preparing to push the co-founder out as CEO, hours after a second affair surfaced, this one with an executive who reports to him. As crazy as it would’ve sounded a few weeks ago, Nvidia without Jensen is no longer unthinkable.
 Reminder:   Our next live workshop is today at 2 PM EST — join Nate Grahek for a free tour of the new all-in-one Claude and the underrated features most users are still missing. RSVP here .

---
 In today’s AI rundown:
 Jensen Huang’s job in doubt after second affair report

 Nate’s Notebook: Claude Projects now take their own notes

 Claim and set up your business on ChatGPT

 Google’s new AlphaGenome traces disease to cells

 LATEST DEVELOPMENTS

 NVIDIA
 🚪  Jensen Huang’s job in doubt after second affair report
 Image source: Creative Commons / The Rundown

 The Rundown: Nvidia’s directors are preparing to remove Jensen Huang as CEO, according to The Wall Street Journal, just hours after The New York Times reported a second affair for the co-founder — this time with a vice president who answers to him.
 The details:
 Five people who’ve worked at Nvidia told the NYT that Jensen and Kimberly Powell, its health care VP, had an affair that’s been discussed internally.

 Jensen’s security reportedly offered an NDA after someone filmed the two being ‘affectionate’ during a March conference, though the NYT hasn’t seen the video.

 The Economist called for Jensen to resign for his involvement with alleged Chinese spy Alice Huang, with members of Congress also pushing for his exit.

 Nvidia lost over $427B in market value in two sessions after the affair came out, rose Wednesday, then fell about 8% after hours as the two reports landed.

 Why it matters: Nvidia ranks among the world’s biggest companies; its chips train nearly every major AI, and almost all of that runs through Jensen. With roughly 60 direct reports and a rockstar persona that customers treat as the company’s face, there’s no playbook for replacing him — and a major shock to the system may be incoming.

 TOGETHER WITH PLAID
 🔌  Plaid powers Finances in ChatGPT

 The Rundown: Plaid’s secure, permissioned data access gives ChatGPT the financial context it needs to give people personalized answers to their money questions. Hear from Ethan Bloch, OpenAI’s Product Lead, Personal Finance, on why secure connectivity and financial context are foundational to the experience.
 When users connect their financial accounts using Plaid, they can ask:
 “Which subscriptions should I cancel?”

 “What would a big trip do to my savings?”

 “Am I being double-charged?”

 Read the full story .

 NATE’S NOTEBOOK
 🗂️ Claude Projects now take their own notes

 The Rundown: Each week, Rundown AI educator Nate Grahek breaks down what he’s seeing while teaching real teams to use AI.
 Nate: Claude Projects on the web can now save their own knowledge files. It went seemingly unnoticed, and I think it matters more than any demo you saw this week.
 You know the demos: Fable 5.2 had 1,000 agents build an entire operating system in eight days. That’s good for clicks, but it doesn’t apply to getting real work done.
 What gets real work done is context. For three years, I’ve taught that Claude needs to know the way you do the work, in your role, at your organization. Set up a Project once with the documents that show how you do a proposal the right way, and it reuses them over and over. On the web, that Project works on any of your devices, and you can share it with your team.
 The catch was that Claude couldn’t add to it. If you wanted Claude to save its research and compare it against next week’s, you had to work locally, and that closed the door on your phone and easy sharing.
 Now, Claude can do the research, synthesize the main ideas, and save them as new knowledge files in the Project. Put it on a schedule, and it’s gathering and curating its own knowledge, both inside and outside your organization.
 Projects have long been Claude’s killer feature, and one tiny detail just made them even better.
 P.S. — If you’re interested in learning about how to utilize Claude to its full potential, join me at today’s free workshop .

 AI TRAINING
 ✅   Claim and set up your business on ChatGPT

 The Rundown: When someone asks ChatGPT about a business like yours, the answer can now draw on details you control. In this guide, you’ll claim your business in ChatGPT Business Hub, verify it, fix what ChatGPT shows, and see how people find you.
 Step-by-step:
 Open Business Hub from the ChatGPT sidebar and search for your business. For now, local stores and restaurants can only claim an existing US listing

 Prove it’s yours with a code sent to the business phone or email, a DNS record on your domain, or your Shopify store. Use whichever option you’re shown

 Complete Persona’s ID check with your government ID and registration details. Edits, insights, and the blue check all wait on Persona’s approval

 Update your description, contact, and policies. OpenAI reviews each change before it appears, and ChatGPT may also use your website, so keep it current

 Open Insights to see mentions, views, and clicks. Eligible US online businesses can also build a business agent; test it in the preview before publishing

 Pro tip: Persona checks your details against official records. Copy your legal name, address, and registration number into a note and paste from there. Typing from memory is how an old address slips in.
 Watch the full guide at The Rundown University →

 PRESENTED BY ARCHERA
 💰 Insurance Backed Guarantee for your cloud spend

 The Rundown: Unpredictable AI workloads make long-term cloud commitments feel like a gamble. Archera lets you commit with a one-time 30-day minimum, then keep or remove the commitment anytime after. If usage drops, an Insurance Backed Guarantee pays you cash back.

 A free FinOps agent and commitment automation

 See your savings without the lock-in .

 GOOGLE DEEPMIND
 🔬  Google’s new AlphaGenome traces disease to cells
 Image source: Google DeepMind

 The Rundown: DeepMind released AlphaGenome 2, an AI that predicts how small DNA differences between people play out inside specific cell types — a more detailed view than the original that could help trace diseases back to the cell types involved.
 The details:
 DeepMind’s Adam Gayoso called it “tying human genetics to cell biology,” as the original version averaged whole tissues while version 2 studies each cell type.

 The original caught just 16% of the DNA changes behind gene shifts in a test on 28 immune cell types, with AlphaGenome 2 nearly doubling it to 30%.

 Labs can also hand it gene activity from just a few dozen cells, like immune cells fired up by a vaccine, and get predictions without having to retrain the model.

 Tested on inflammatory bowel disease, the model matched a recent study by picking out a DNA change that overworks one gene in the gut’s immune cells.

 Why it matters: Scientists have found plenty of DNA quirks tied to diseases like type 2 diabetes, but they often can’t tell which cells they actually impact — the part drug makers need. AlphaGenome 2 helps answer that question and identify the experiments worth running first, which could mean better-aimed treatments for common illnesses.

 COMMUNITY AI WORKFLOW OF THE DAY

 Today’s workflow comes from reader Arun Sriraman:
 “I use this workflow to turn a recording of a badminton match into a coaching session for individual players. It's for coaches and players who want written and spoken feedback on a specific player’s performance without writing the analysis from scratch.
 Share the analysis output with an LLM such as Gemini or Claude and ask it to turn the output into a human-sounding coaching narrative. Convert the narrative to speech with TTS, then video encode the coaching session.
 The end result is a narrated coaching session video for the player under review, ready to share with them.”

blogs.title: When the Central Bank of AI Changes Chairs
blogs.description:
Read on tomtunguz.com → For the past four years, Jensen Huang ran the Central Bank of AI. Today he resigned as chief executive of Nvidia.1

Wh…
blogs.content:
Read on tomtunguz.com →
 For the past four years, Jensen Huang ran the Central Bank of AI. Today he resigned as chief executive of Nvidia. 1

 What are the implications for the AI economy?

 1. If the Central Bank of AI tightens policy, the AI economy slows. Over the past two years, Nvidia committed $42b to M&A & technology buyouts, 2 invested $61b of cash on a cost basis into equity stakes across 229 startups & 13 public companies, 3 & extended $164.5b in lease guarantees & cloud capacity backstops that require capital reserves alongside $63.1b in customer receivables, where payment terms now stretch up to a full year. 4 5 Under a more financially disciplined regime facing heightened board scrutiny, any tightening of those equity checks, payment terms or lease backstops will slow AI buildouts just as the broader economy slows when the Federal Reserve tightens credit.

 2. Nvidia fused the startup & chip ecosystems in a way we have never seen. Under Huang, Nvidia acted simultaneously as chip supplier, lead venture investor, anchor cloud customer & lease guarantor across more than 200 startups. Those deals ran on Huang’s personal conviction & relationships. Nvidia now needs a leader who can sustain these founder partnerships without the co-founder who built them.

 3. Open-source startups lose their primary patron & buyer. Nvidia has been the single largest buyer & financier of American open-source AI companies, committing $22b to its Nemotron stack across Hugging Face, Poolside & Essential AI : no other company has bought open-source teams at scale. 6 Meta, Google & at least eight US startups that have raised $100m or more continue to train open-weight models, 7 & they will now have to carry more of the American open-source mantle themselves.

 4. Tighter export controls. The episode likely increases pressure in Washington for stricter semiconductor export controls & compliance rules.

 5. An opening for custom silicon. Custom AI ASICs already account for 28% of AI server shipments & 15% to 20% of accelerator revenue in 2026, led by Google’s TPUs at 65% of the custom silicon market alongside AWS’s Trainium3, Meta’s MTIA & Broadcom’s custom XPUs. 8 Leadership turbulence at a single-source supplier accelerates that shift.

 The change of leadership at the Central Bank of AI is a pivotal moment for the industry. It is hard to overstate how central Nvidia has become to startup financing, M&A exits & policy across the fastest-growing segment of the US economy. A sudden transition at the top introduces real uncertainty into the market & especially in startups.

---

 Nvidia 2025 & 2026 M&A & strategic technology buyouts ($42b total) : Groq ($20.0b LPU technology license & engineering acqui-hire, December 2025, with $13.0b paid in Q4 FY26 & $2.94b in Q2 FY27 per SEC filings), Hugging Face ($12.93b acquisition announced September 3, 2026), Poolside ($6.0b Model Factory non-exclusive license & transfer of 109 Laguna engineers into Nemotron, August 2026), Enfabrica ($900m networking license & team, September 2025), Run:ai ($700m), Gretel ($320m), Deci ($300m), Shoreline ($100m), Brev, SchedMD, CentML & Essential AI (June 2026).  ↩︎

 Nvidia Form 10-K (FY26) & Form 10-Q for the second quarter ended July 26, 2026 (filed August 26, 2026) : cumulative cash paid for purchases of equity securities over the last eight quarters totals $60.8b on a cost basis ($1.49b in FY25, $17.50b in FY26 & $42.40b in 1H FY27, with an additional $25.0b in pending equity commitments). Including $34.3b of cumulative unrealized mark-to-market gains ($10.6b in FY26 & $23.7b in 1H FY27), the carrying fair value on Nvidia’s balance sheet reached $94.0b to $99.0b across 229 private companies & 13 public companies. Disclosed stakes include $30.0b in OpenAI, up to $10.0b in Anthropic, SpaceX/xAI, CoreWeave, Safe Superintelligence, Intel, Nebius, Synopsys & Poolside.  ↩︎

 Nvidia Q2 FY27 Form 10-Q off-balance-sheet commitments ($530.5b total across supply, cloud & guarantee obligations) & Note 7 (Supplemental Financial Statement Information) : contingent credit & capacity backstops total $164.5b, comprising $108.5b in lease & debt default guarantees (led by an up-to-$105.0b backstop on OpenAI’s Ohio data center leases with SB Energy), $36.0b in multi-year neocloud take-or-pay capacity agreements (including CoreWeave’s $6.3b residual capacity guarantee through 2032 & Lambda’s $1.5b agreement) & $20.0b in 15-year data center leases signed by Nvidia for reassignment to neocloud partners. While off balance sheet unless triggered, these guarantees require Nvidia to maintain substantial liquidity reserves. On the balance sheet, accounts receivable jumped from $38.5b at FY26 end to $63.1b in Q2 FY27 (consuming $24.6b of operating cash flow in six months), with five customers representing 70% of receivables (22%, 14%, 13%, 11% & 10%). Days sales outstanding (DSO) stretched from a 47.8-day 10-year historical average to 60 to 65 days as Note 7 disclosed extended payment terms ranging from 90 days up to one full year to finance customer data center builds.  ↩︎

 Over the past four quarters, Nvidia generated $134.4b in operating cash flow & put $75.8b straight into equity stakes & acquisitions : peaking last quarter at $27.0b, or 112% of operating cash flow. Nvidia Condensed Consolidated Statements of Cash Flows (Form 10-K for FY26 ended January 25, 2026 & Form 10-Q for Q1 & Q2 FY27 ended July 26, 2026). Quarterly operating cash flow vs. cash outflows into equity securities & acquisitions/Groq buyout : Q3 FY25 (+$17.63b OCF vs. -$0.76b deployed, 4%), Q4 FY25 (+$16.63b vs. -$1.02b, 6%), Q1 FY26 (+$27.41b vs. -$1.03b, 4%), Q2 FY26 (+$15.37b vs. -$0.89b, 6%), Q3 FY26 (+$23.75b vs. -$4.15b, 18%), Q4 FY26 (+$36.19b vs. -$25.97b, 72%), Q1 FY27 (+$50.34b vs. -$18.67b, 37%) & Q2 FY27 (+$24.08b vs. -$26.98b, 112%).  ↩︎

 Nvidia’s $22b open-source & Nemotron commitments combine the $12.93b Hugging Face acquisition (September 2026), the $7.0b Poolside deal ($6.0b Model Factory license + $1.0b equity round, August 2026), the acqui-hire of Essential AI (founded by Transformer co-authors Ashish Vaswani & Niki Parmar, June 2026) & $2.0b in Nemotron Alliance open-weight model & dataset grants.  ↩︎

 US startups that have raised at least $100m to train open-weight models include Thinking Machines Lab ($2.0b seed at $40b valuation, shipping Inkling open models), Poolside ($1.6b+ raised at $12b valuation), Together AI ($530m+ raised at $7.5b valuation), Liquid AI ($250m+ raised at $2.3b valuation, Liquid Foundation Models), Arcee AI ($150m+ Series B in September 2026 at $1b valuation), Reflection AI ($130m+ raised, shipping the 501b-parameter open-weight Beam model in October 2026), Prime Intellect ($130m Series A in July 2026 at $1b valuation, INTELLECT models) & Deep Cogito ($100m+ raised, Cogito-v2.1-671B open-weight model).  ↩︎

Within custom silicon, Google TPU holds 64.8% to 65.1% share, followed by AWS Trainium & Inferentia (14.6%), Meta MTIA (8.7%), Microsoft Maia (6.4%) & OpenAI/emerging programs (5.5%).  ↩︎

blogs.name: Tim Kellogg
blogs.title: Knowledge Graphs
blogs.description: Not gonna lie, I hate knowledge graphs. Not long ago, this post would have been about why they’re terrible (and they are, there’s truth in…
blogs.content:
Not gonna lie, I hate knowledge graphs . Not long ago, this post would have been about why they’re terrible (and
they are, there’s truth in this). But I’ve come to realize that there’s some very good reasons to use knowledge
graphs in AI. I’ll walk you through my arc, maybe you can appreciate them too.

 What’s a KG?

 A knowledge graph (KG) is a special type of graph database where the nodes are entities (nouns) and the edges are
 relationships . Typically both the entities & relationships also can have properties .

 Narrator: Yo, it’s not necessary to legit use a graph DB engine, SQL works fine for almost anyone.

 The promise of KGs was that they can express logic that you can do proofs on, or infer results that might not
have been obvious at first. It’s a rich , flexible data model around potentially gnarly domains. Also, you
can use them to ground LLMs.

 Why don’t I like them?

 They’re not bitter lesson pilled.

 The Bitter Lesson was an essay to AI researchers stating that the methods that work best in AI are those
that get better as compute improves .

 I’ve commonly conflated the Bitter Lesson with agents — if you’re building
an agent and a new model drops that’s 2x as good, does your agent also get 2x as good? If not, then your design
isn’t Bitter Lesson pilled and you’ll fall behind quickly. It follows the same logic as the Bitter Lesson, but
technically incorrect.

 Models are getting better regardless if you want them to, no effort on your part. Like a force of nature. So
effort is better spent on multiplying LLM gains (that will happen anyway) rather than trying to big-brain the
smartest solution.

 Knowledge graphs are notoriously difficult to construct. They frequently take PhD-level experts and lots of
design to get the KG schema (ontology) constructed well. The Bitter Lesson directly warns against methods that
require investing in complex designs (yes, knowledge graphs).

 Brittleness

 You can tell you’re dealing with a system that’s not Bitter Lesson pilled when you bump into incorrect assumptions
about the real world. Things don’t feel right, broken.

 The problem with knowledge graphs is they’re inherently limited to what a single human can conceive, and usually
far more limited than that. Like with code. Code that has a lot of if statements and edge cases gets super
complex real fast. Same with knowledge graphs for a really similar reason, you’re effectively hand-coding the
domain, so it all has to fit into someone’s head.

 And so they’re lossy. Read any good book on designing ontologies or knowledge graphs and this is the first thing
 — they convince you to accept that it can’t be perfect , so just focus on the highest value things.

 Which is where the problems stem from. The “highest value thing” is what someone somewhere (more likely, a committee
of people) thought was the most valuable, and frequently misses a thing you thought was important.

 But they’re good

 Alas, I do like knowledge graphs! They’re really good when you need systematic repeatable completeness.

 For example, ARTEX (not giving you a direct link
because it’s an offensive cybersecurity tool, but here is an example of it being used ). It uses two
graphs (technically not knowledge graphs). One graph keeps track of assets like IP addresses, apps, services,
ports, etc. The other graph is for exploration and stores things like goals, findings, observations, etc.

 ARTEX is basically a very Claude Code like tool that uses these graphs to fan out and completely saturate every
asset with every possible vulnerability in effort to find a way in.

 I’ve started using a KG-like graph for tracking AI news & developments. It’s got:

 Entity types: Person, Organization, Model, Software, Hardware, Research Artifact, Policy, Place, Concept, Security Incident, Security Issue, Mitigation

 Relationship types: has metric, compared with, released, developed by, criticisizes, questions, affects, comments about, predicts, mitigated by, announces, reports, advocates, recommends, uses method, proposes, supports, assesses, has price, has failure, restricts

 One of the core principles with this project is that it doesn’t store facts, it just stores observations.
The factuality is determined at query time.

 The most exciting thing that happened with this was that I told an agent to “let me know if anything surprising happens”, where
 “surprising” is defined as anything that conflicts with the conventional knowledge of the graph. It proceeded
to spend the next 12 hours giving me updates on truly surprising things that I wouldn’t have otherwise caught.

 This stuff is easy with graphs.

 In the past
I’ve tried to get agents to do this with just plain-text storage and it’s just really hard. To do it well, you have
to add so much prompting to describe what “surprising ” looks like that you’ve effectively designed a KG ontology.
So even though it’s just relying on LLMs, it doesn’t feel any more Bitter Lesson pilled.

 Where KGs work best

 Current LLMs seem to do poorly with systematically listing ideas or processing edge cases & states.

 If you want it to check for “all the bad things” , they do
a whole lot better if you give them a list of all the things you consider bad. At least it gives you a lot
more consistent behavior. It’s possible, just not great.

 KGs work best when they’re filling in for the weaknesses of LLMs. If you only store prose journal entries, they’ll
inconsistently find observations of a certain type. Part of the problem is every time you have to re-evaluate
the list, the LLM has to completely re-discover the observations. And that re-discovery introduces fluctuations
in behavior.

 Will this change?

 I’m not sure. It’s hard to predict where AI is going to go next.

 One thing on my mind is that KGs can be processed via code. And code is hella cheaper and faster than any
LLM interaction will ever be.

 I have a theory that the general public, in the long run, may rarely interact directly with
AI. Instead, they’ll interact with code that’s written, maintained, and operated by AI agents. They still get that
dynamic feel, because the code quickly adapts to what they need. But it’s fundamentally just code.
KGs are analogous to data-level code, and so they’re a great tool for AI to inject it’s own intelligence into
plain code.

 I have no idea if that’s a realistic future, but there’s good reasons to think it might be. It’s certainly cheap
and a whole lot more scalable.

 When predicting which technology or technique wins out, a lot of times it’s actually social factors that determine
fate. And in this case, those social factors could just be that KGs are cheap and scalable. And using AI to maintain
the KG would convey most of the dynamism benefits.

 Conclusion

 Well anyway, do what you want. Be cautious with knowledge graphs. Be bitter lesson pilled. But also be aware of LLM
weaknesses. They could be a good solution!

blogs.title: An Interview With Roblox CEO David Baszucki About Aggregating Play
blogs.author: Ben Thompson
blogs.description: An interview with Roblox CEO David Baszucki about how AI is transforming game creation, and why that opens up huge opportunities to both enable developers and make Roblox both an Aggregator and a platform.
blogs.content:
An interview with Roblox CEO David Baszucki about how AI is transforming game creation, and why that opens up huge opportunities to both enable developers and make Roblox both an Aggregator and a platform.

---

Listen to this Update in your podcast player

---

Good morning,

This week’s Stratechery Interview is with Roblox CEO David Baszucki . I’ve interviewed Baszucki twice, in February 2022 , and November 2023 .

What struck me about this interview is just how much AI has changed the landscape for Roblox. This was a company predicated on the concept that anyone can make a game, but now, for the first time, literally anyone can make a game. That means a world of abundance, and in that world, there is an opportunity to be an Aggregator, and Roblox is aggressively pursuing that opportunity.

To that end, we discuss how AI has changed Baszucki’s view of what is possible, what goes into a game creation harness, making games on your phone, and the power of recommendation. Then we talk about Roblox’s vision of a universal player, where a Roblox game works everywhere, and Roblox Everywhere, where Roblox developers can use the platform beyond the Roblox app. We also touch on advertising — the natural Aggregator business model — and whether Baszucki still thinks he is building the metaverse.

As a reminder, all Stratechery content, including interviews, is available as a podcast; click the link at the top of this email to add Stratechery to your podcast player.

On to the Interview:

An Interview With Roblox CEO David Baszucki About Aggregating Play

This interview is lightly edited for clarity.

Topics: The AI Impact | A Game Creation Harness | Roblox Build | Roblox Discovery | Universal Player | Roblox Everywhere | Advertising | Metaverses

The AI Impact

David Baszucki, welcome back to Stratechery.

DB: Thank you, Ben, for having me back. It’s great to be here.

So this is the third time I’ve interviewed you, and I want to sort of put that in an interesting context. First, you started Roblox in 2004, you went public in 2021, you first talked to me in 2022 and again in 2023 , that’s like a nearly 20-year stretch. Now it’s 2026, and here’s my question: Is the world more different for you now, compared to three years before, than it was for the entire first two decades from starting the company to the last time we talked?

DB: The changes in the world we all feel are sure happening a lot more rapidly. When we first published Roblox — I don’t know if people on this podcast remember — software used to be distributed on floppy disks and CDs.

You know, the funny thing is, you’re the second person I’ve interviewed in the last two or three weeks where we’ve referenced back to fact that the reason we say packaged software is it used to actually be packaged!

DB: It’s been crazy, we had the Internet, when we started the company, we had the vision of a category called immersive co-experience, sci-fi writers have been writing about the holodeck forever, and we went along our way.

I’m still pro-metaverse, we can use the word metaverse, it’s okay.

DB: Okay, good, we use them all. It’s Snow Crash — metaverse, holodeck, they’re all good. We started on this vision of building human co-experience, we saw the mobile age come across us, we saw the crypto age. The AI acceleration wave we’re in is faster and bigger and crazier than anything I’ve ever seen, it’s changing how we think about the product, it’s changing how people are going to create games. What’s really exciting is, when we started the company, we had this slogan called “You Make the Game”.

Yep.

DB: We started with that slogan, we learned along the way that the ratio of people who might want to play games to make games has drifted — more people want to just play games than make games, because historically making games has been Roblox Studio and 3D editing and writing script.

We could be approaching the time where “You Make the Game” really comes true, and where making a game is accessible to everyone. It’s really fun, I’ll tell you a bit about some of the experiments we’ve been having with Roblox Build . But we’re entering an era where making a game could be as big as playing a game.

I’m right there with you. We’re obviously going to touch on all those points, I think it’s probably predictable what we want to talk about. But to go back to 2023, you called AI then, “a super paintbrush and a super 3D modeler, rather than a full replacement” — Is that still how you’re thinking about AI?

DB: It’s what the data is proving out. We just had our earnings call a few weeks ago , we highlighted a lot of acceleration. One, there’s various ways humans can augment with AI on Roblox, they can use MCP , which is like plugging in a model, they can use the Roblox AI assistant to help build.

And what do you mean with that MCP server? You mentioned you had 5x growth quarter-over-quarter. That’s where you’re actually using Claude Code or Codex or whatever to work with Roblox?

DB: People are plugging in, we can see all of them — Claude Code, Codex, other models — all being plugged into Roblox Studio to help build things. We’ve seen two games hit the top 20 made by AI, we have other metrics like the number of assets.

What do you mean by “made by AI”? Because you also said 80% of games in the top 100 have AI-contributed content.

DB: Touched by AI, vibe-coded directly with AI, and we can see the count of assets accelerating.

Got it.

DB: It’s turned out to be, I believe, somewhat faithful to what I said. This is a human paintbrush accelerator, good ideas are still very important, novel types of gameplay are very important. But people are able to flex their creativity much more quickly. We have members of the Roblox board of directors carrying a mobile phone around, building games like 15 times a day. We have people who are not necessarily engineers or product managers now building within the company, so we’re really at the dawn of a new era.

A Game Creation Harness

You mentioned the super paintbrush, super 3D modeler, is there a super gameplay developer? Because there’s a large step between, “I have an idea for a game”, versus the actual mechanics of the game. How much can the AI do to help you as far as that goes?

DB: You’re touching on the dream of what is a game creation harness versus a coding harness .

Dive into it, this is super interesting. Lay out the difference and the way you’re thinking about that.

DB: So everyone’s getting familiar with coding harnesses — Claude Code, Cursor, Replit, Lovable, Codex, you name it. A game is arguably much more complicated than code. As you mentioned, there’s art, there’s 3D objects, there’s scenes, there’s avatars, there can be gameplay code, there can be missions, and there can be code underneath it. So a harness that is being created to create games really has to run in multiple modalities, needs to listen to you, and if you said, “I would like a multiplayer tortoise-and-the-hare game that 100 people can play, and we’d like to do it on Venus, and I’d like it to run on all devices” — there’s a lot of different things that need to be generated there.

The avatars, the assets, all of that, as well as the gameplay, which I think is a very human thing — your idea of what type of a game it is is actually very unique. So one of our board members is building a hybrid kind of Wordle-crossword game with his own vision of how this crossword game should work, and that’s very unique to him. I’m optimistic we’re still seeing that notion of a human coupled with an accelerating paintbrush in essentially a very complex harness for building games.

There’s so many pieces you talked about. The asset creation piece, compared to 2023, much further along, arguably there. You could have even the video component, or the moving worlds, but then you almost have these different pieces. Do you have to build — is there going to be one harness, and one sort of — we’re going to get to your Build app in a little bit — that handles all of that? Or are you still thinking we need to do this piece-by-piece as the model gets good enough for, or we need different models maybe for the different parts of this?

DB: I think just as we see with harnesses that are routing different models, even for coding now, a lot of companies have multiple models running side-by-side and their harness is optimizing. Our harness inside Build and inside Studio Build is running not just multiple models for certain things, but then there’s a second dimension of, “Are we building a scene?”, “Are we building a 3D object?”, “Are we building code?”, “Are we building an NPC?”.

So yes, we are routing both by kind of specific asset that’s being created, as well as multiple models within each of those, and we’re combining some areas where we have incredible data on Roblox — for example, data that can be used to help create non-player characters, characters that act normally, side-by-side with you. But there’s also really good coding models out there, both open source and frontier, and so we see a harness being able to put all these things together.

What’s the mix of those models? Say we have three categories — frontier, off-the-shelf open-source models, and models that you’ve trained specifically. And I guess even there there’s two categories, are you doing foundational models on your own, or just doing some post-training?

DB: We literally have all three of those running in our Build harness. And we’re, in certain cases, optimizing the cost of frontier with the capabilities of open source. We have a Cube model — we’ve announced it — which is trained on 3D assets.

Yeah, super interesting. Tell me about the Cube model.
